newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa seeks foster homes for 4,000 children.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa seeks foster homes for 4,000 children.

text.p: Mother Teresa, rapidly gaining strength after life-saving surgery last week, met new members of her Missionaries of Charity religious order on Thursday, took a brief stroll and said she planned to return to work soon.
But uppermost in Mother Teresa's mind was the fate of 4,000 children whom she is trying to place with foster families, a clinic official told a news conference.
"She was in a very cheerful mood," said A.K. Chatterjee, administrator of Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre, where Mother Teresa is being treated.
He said the legendary missionary asked for his help in finding good foster homes for the children.

"She told me..."they have to be adopted by good families. Tomorrow you come to me,'" Chatterjee quoted the Roman Catholic nun as saying. When he reminded her that she had to get well first, she insisted that she was fine.
"No I'm absolutely fine," Chatterjee quoted her as saying. "Tomorrow I think I'll go home."
Chatterjee added: "She was in a very good mood and she was blessing everybody, holding hands and things like that."
Earlier, the 86-year-old nun took a short 20-foot (6 metre) stroll outside her room in the clinic's intensive therapy unit, supported by a doctor and a nurse, he said.

A late night bulletin said Mother Teresa had practised walking for 10 minutes in the evening. She ate chicken soup, cheese sandwiches, fruit salad, chocolate custard and sandesh, a milk-based sweet, for dinner, clinic officials said.
"She is now having physiotherapy," the bulletin said.
The 1979 Nobel peace prize winner walked her first few steps on Wednesday after surgery to clear two blocked arteries last Friday.

On Thursday morning, Mother Teresa met about 40 new members of the order she founded, the Missionaries of Charity, and blessed them, Chatterjee said. "They visited Mother Teresa for about 15 minutes."
Later the new nuns took their final vows in a simple ceremony at the nearby St Mary's Church.
Doctors said Mother Teresa was not yet out of danger.
Thursday's noon medical bulletin said: "We truly do not have any estimate of her time of recovery. We could still encounter setbacks and complications."
Doctors had hoped to release Mother Teresa by the weekend. But Chatterjee said they had decided against this, preferring to wait until she had spent five or six days in "steady equilibrium".

Mother Teresa's post-operative condition was complicated by an irregular heartbeat, bronchial pneumonia and long-standing kidney and lung problems. Last Friday marked her third round of heart-related surgery in five years.
Doctors believe her recovery will take a long time and say Mother Teresa, who was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989, may never be as active as before.
Despite numerous health problems, Mother Teresa had kept a hectic schedule as head of her religious order and had travelled widely. The order's 4,500 members run 456 homes in 111 nations.
